primary_topics: Art's first decade on the Supreme Court (1995-2005) -- entering the neo-classical Padre Faura building designed by Filipino architect Antonio Toledo under the 1905 Burnham Plan, flanked by the bronze statues of Chief Justices Cayetano Arellano and José Abad Santos and the Court's seal with the scales of justice resting on the Ten Commandments tablets ('the origins of the Philippine legal system which draws from Judeo-Christian ethos'). Art unclogged dockets with 'seemingly boundless energy,' becoming 'the most prolific writer in the history of the Supreme Court.'

The death-penalty crusade -- Art's separate opinions in People v. Esparas and Libed (Aug 20, 1996; 260 SCRA 552) and People v. Echegaray (G.R. No. 117472, Feb 7, 1997) opposing Republic Act 7659 as unconstitutional and quoting Pope John Paul II's Evangelium Vitae ('A Hymn to Human Life'): 'punishment... ought not to go to the extreme of executing the offender except in cases of absolute necessity... very rare, if not practically nonexistent.' His persistence drew impeachment threats from Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa for the 'crusade against capital punishment even for heinous crimes' -- Art persisted, and 'though the Court upheld the Death Penalty Law, new jurisprudence stipulated that imprisonment and not the death penalty was the recourse for cases up for review.' The case rested only when President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo signed Republic Act 9346 abolishing the death penalty on June 24, 2006.

The Family Code Article 36 psychological-incapacity guidelines -- as ponente of Republic v. Court of Appeals and Molina (G.R. No. 108763, Feb 13, 1997), Art was tasked by the Office of the Solicitor General with standardizing the interpretation of 'psychological incapacity' as a ground for nullity. He invited Archbishop Oscar V. Cruz (head of the Philippine National Appellate Matrimonial Tribunal) as Amicus Curiae -- not from devotional preference but because the concept itself was sourced from Canon Law -- and, building on the earlier Santos v. Court of Appeals (January 1995) holding (gravity, juridical antecedence, incurability), crafted eight guidelines that drew complaints of strictness but which Art defended on the explicit ground that 'psychological incapacity as a ground to nullify a marriage was copied by the Family Code from Canon Law.'

Art's doctrine of church-state separation that is not separation-from-God -- 'the Philippines is theist, not atheist, not even agnostic; in fact, it is monotheistic; it worships one God,' citing the Constitution's preamble ('We, the sovereign Filipino people, imploring the aid of Almighty God...') and the practice of both chambers of Congress invoking the divine before sessions. The doctrine concretely produced the Centennial Prayer for the Courts that Art composed with Chief Justice Davide for the 100th anniversary of the Supreme Court -- a non-mandatory opening invocation respecting non-believing justices but adopted by a 'significant number.'

Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide as Art's praying-magistrate counterpart -- 3:30 AM Bible reading as daily practice, integrity / wisdom / humility / patriotism / 'righteousness' as Art's catalog of his virtues -- and the chapter's closing foreshadow of the January 2001 Estrada impeachment crisis they would navigate together, 'guided by the Constitution and Bible readings,' setting up Chapter 12.

stances.claim: Art's opposition to the death penalty was framed as constitutional and theological in equal measure -- Republic Act 7659 was 'unconstitutional' AND in 'direct opposition to the sixth commandment.' The Echegaray separate opinion explicitly cites the Pope's Evangelium Vitae alongside Philippine constitutional argument. The biography presents this not as a category error but as Art's settled position that constitutional and natural-law reasoning converge on the same conclusion.
stances.rhetorical_move: convergence argument; constitutional and theological coextensiveness

stances.claim: Faced with Chief Justice Narvasa's impeachment threat for relentless death-penalty dissent, Art responded by invoking his providential appointment: 'his ascent to the highest court of the land was a stroke of the Divine; he was beholden to no one else but God.' The biography treats this as both a personal explanation and a doctrine of judicial independence rooted not in institutional position but in divine commission.
stances.rhetorical_move: providential warrant as guarantee of judicial independence

stances.claim: The Molina guidelines, though derived from Canon Law via Archbishop Cruz, are defended by Art on textualist grounds -- the Family Code itself copied the concept of psychological incapacity from Canon Law, so Canon Law is the proper interpretive source. The biography uses this as the test case for Art's distinctive ability to ground religious-conceptual borrowing in straightforward legal reasoning without confessional advocacy.
stances.rhetorical_move: textualist defense of religiously sourced concept

stances.claim: Art's church-state doctrine threads a needle: separation OF church and state, but not separation of state FROM God. The state is neutral among denominations, but the Constitution is theist (preamble), the legislature invokes the divine, and the optional Centennial Prayer for the Courts is permissible. The doctrine refuses both confessional-state and atheist-state readings of the Constitution.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal threading; refusal of two opposing extremes

stances.claim: Davide and Art are presented as the 'praying-magistrate' typology -- distinct from their colleagues in their public dependence on Scripture for daily orientation. The chapter quietly establishes that this typology will produce the decisive January 2001 EDSA II / Estrada resolution that Chapter 12 will narrate.
stances.rhetorical_move: typological pairing; biographical setup for the next chapter

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 chronicles Art's first decade on the Supreme Court (1995-2005) as Associate Justice, opening with the neo-classical Padre Faura building designed by Filipino architect Antonio Toledo under Daniel Burnham's 1905 Manila plan -- its four pillars, its bronze Arellano and Abad Santos statues, and its court seal with scales of justice resting on the Ten Commandments tablets symbolizing 'the origins of the Philippine legal system which draws from Judeo-Christian ethos.' Art entered with 'seemingly boundless energy,' becoming by tenure-end 'the most prolific writer in the history of the Supreme Court' -- coherent full-length decisions, minute resolutions, no case left undecided, all 'mindful to resolve each dispute with fairness and equitability.' Three signature lines of work define the chapter. First, the death-penalty crusade: separate opinions in People v. Esparas and Libed (Aug 20, 1996; 260 SCRA 552) and People v. Echegaray (G.R. No. 117472, Feb 7, 1997) argued Republic Act 7659 unconstitutional and in direct opposition to the sixth commandment, citing Pope John Paul II's Evangelium Vitae that capital punishment is justifiable only in cases 'very rare, if not practically nonexistent.' Even Chief Justice Narvasa's impeachment threat could not dissuade Art, who held that 'his ascent to the highest court of the land was a stroke of the Divine' and he was 'beholden to no one else but God.' Though outvoted on constitutionality, Art produced a procedural workaround -- new jurisprudence holding that imprisonment, not death, was the recourse for cases under review -- and only when President Arroyo signed Republic Act 9346 on June 24, 2006 did 'Art rest his case.' Second, the Family Code Article 36 guidelines: as ponente of Republic v. Court of Appeals and Molina (G.R. No. 108763, Feb 13, 1997), tasked by the Office of the Solicitor General with standardizing the interpretation of 'psychological incapacity' as a nullity ground, Art invited Archbishop Oscar V. Cruz -- head of the National Appellate Matrimonial Tribunal of the Philippine Church -- as Amicus Curiae, not from devotional preference but because the concept itself was sourced from Canon Law. Building on Santos v. Court of Appeals (Jan 1995)'s baseline of 'gravity, juridical antecedence and incurability,' Art crafted eight guidelines that drew complaints of strictness but which he defended on the explicit textual ground that 'psychological incapacity as a ground to nullify a marriage was copied by the Family Code from Canon Law.' Third, the church-state threading: Art held uncompromisingly to separation of church and state -- neutrality among denominations, no public funds for any church group, no establishment -- while insisting that 'there is no separation of the state from God,' citing the Constitution's preamble ('We, the sovereign Filipino people, imploring the aid of Almighty God...') and the fact that both chambers of Congress invoked the divine before sessions. Concretely, the doctrine produced the Centennial Prayer for the Courts that Art composed with Chief Justice Davide for the Supreme Court's 100th anniversary -- optional and respectful of non-believing justices, but adopted by a 'significant number.' The chapter closes by introducing Davide as Art's 'praying-magistrate' counterpart -- a 3:30 AM Bible reader, possessed of 'integrity, wisdom, humility, patriotism, keen sense of righteousness' -- and foreshadowing the January 2001 Estrada impeachment crisis they would jointly navigate 'guided by the Constitution and Bible readings,' setting up Chapter 12.
